catalog_quote: Stress in Yurakaré falls either on the penultimate or the antepenultimate syllable of a word. There is a basic stress rule, which I will discuss in section 2.4.1. There are many exceptions to this stress rule, but these exceptions show patterns as well. ... In the normal case, starting from the left edge of a word, every second syllable is stressed; the rightmost of these stressed syllables gets primary stress. In other words: a regular word in Yurakaré is built up out of binary feet with a right dominant node (iambic). Main stress falls on the rightmost dominant node of a word. The word-final syllable is never stressed, even if a strict application of the rule given above would lead to a stressed final syllable. I consider the final syllable to be extrametrical ... [2.4.3] Apparently, the stress-attracting prefix(-cluster)-rule can be overruled by penultimate closed syllables. Three-syllable words with an initial heavy syllable get stress on the first syllable when they do not carry affixes ... For heavy penultimate syllables, the 'stress heavy syllable' rule is respected, and foot structure is ignored. ... When both the penultimate and antepenultimate syllable are heavy, the penultimate will be stressed ... Further research is needed to determine the exact role heaviness plays and the conditions involved. ... [2.4.4] primary stress in Yurakaré falls maximally two syllables to the left of the right edge of a word.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Parse the word into iambic (right-headed) binary feet from the left edge with the final syllable extrametrical; primary stress goes to the head of the rightmost foot, so it lands on the penult in even-parity words (pojóre 'canoe') and on the antepenult in odd-parity words (tipójore 'my canoe'); a stress window keeps primary stress within two syllables of the right edge. Syllable weight interferes: a closed (heavy) penult attracts stress even over stress-attracting prefixes (ta-báshti 'our wife'), trisyllables with a heavy initial syllable stress it (púydara, bállata), and when both penult and antepenult are heavy the penult wins; a set of plural/object prefixes (ta-, pa-, ma-, ka-, li-, la-, co-operative object prefixes) carry lexical foot heads and pull stress to the initial syllable (tá-sibë 'our house' vs ti-síbë 'my house').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: every foot head from the left carries stress, the rightmost being primary, the others secondary (tà-sibë́=chi, tà-pojóre, tàlipá-newe 'chicken-dirt'); stress-attracting prefixes can carry secondary stress when a later foot head takes primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final disyllabic suffixes/enclitics are never stressed (ti-memé-shama, së́-tina); question words strongly prefer initial stress, with repair by syncope (tëtë-bëshë > të́tëpshë); diacritically marked roots, mostly Spanish/Quechua loans, keep their own stress (ti-mésa, ta-mésa, tà-pantálu, tálipa 'chicken', shínama, lë́jëlë, látiji); stress-avoiding syllables (singular possessive prefixes ti-/mi-/a-, some root-initial syllables) refuse stress and geminate the following consonant when forced to carry it (dójjo 'body' vs ti-dójo, tá-dojo); monosyllabic roots copy their vowel to avoid final stress (pá.a 'younger brother'); a few possessed monosyllables stress the prefix (tí-nñu, tí-bba); discourse highlighting can shift stress (latíjsha ~ látijsha) and intonation-phrase pitch can override all rules, stressing the penult or even the final syllable of a medial clause; ideophones may have final stress (6.6.2). Author notes heaviness effects need further research.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (phonological) word including prefixes, suffixes and enclitics, compounds and reduplications; van Gijn 2014 (abstract) frames it as the phonological word, interacting with morphology and syntax. Word-level stress is not contrastive; pragmatic stress is not grammaticalized. Examples are from elicited citation forms and narrative texts. Reading chosen as 'weight-sensitive' because the primary mechanism is a left-to-right iambic count bounded by a right-edge window (not a fixed position), with syllable weight and morpheme-specific (prefix/root) marking as the stated modulating factors.
new_statements.identity_note: van Gijn 2006 describes Yurakaré as a whole (fieldwork in the Chapare/Sécure/Isiboro area, 2000s) and states (p. 2-3) that no author since d'Orbigny (1839) has found dialect subdivisions; the two historical groupings Mansiños/Solostos correspond to Glottolog dialects mans1263 and solo1241 but the grammar does not tie its data to either. The statement applies to the language-level languoid yura1255.

tone.quote: Yurakaré has a so-called morphological accent system, in which “surface stress is the result of a complex interplay of stem type (accented versus unaccented) and diacritic properties of affixes” (Hayes 1995:32). Yurakaré has a default rhythmic pattern (iambic left-to-right with weight sensitivity), but a number of often morpheme-specific rules that influence this basic pattern. [...] in certain pragmatic circumstances word-final syllables can be accented. This is arguably not word stress, but rather intonational or utterance accent.

tone.quote: Stress in Yurakaré is rather complex and interacts with morphology. The default stress pattern is based on a iambic foot structure constructed from left to right, with the main stress falling on the rightmost foot head. Words are usually not stressed on the last syllable. Van Gijn (2006:38) considers the last syllable extrametrical. [...] The pattern is further complicated by interaction of stress with syllable weight (cf. van Gijn 2006:40-1) and utterance intonation. Pragmatic factors also seem to play a role in some cases.
